---
title: "Figure 10.2: LA7: General Government Structural Primary Balance"
---

![Python: `python/fig-10-2.py`](../images/python/fig-10-2.png)

Three vintages of World Economic Outlook (WEO) projections for the same
variable, the structural primary balance of LA7 governments. Each line is
the forecast as it was made at one point in time: October 2025, April 2026
and October 2026. Comparing them shows how the projections have been
revised. The vintages are shown in shades of purple with different line
styles, so the newest stands out.

**New in this chart:** solid, dashed and dotted lines.

## The data

Sheet `data`, 11 rows (2021 to 2031):

| category | October 2026 WEO | April 2026 WEO | October 2025 WEO |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2021 | -2.69 | -2.71 | -2.64 |

One column per vintage, with the years as numbers. The early years are
history, so the three vintages are nearly identical there; they diverge in
the projection years.

## The script

### Colours and line styles

```python
# Each vintage of the projections: (colour, line style).
vintages = {
    "October 2026 WEO": ("#5B267A", "solid"),
    "April 2026 WEO": ("#8752AA", (0, (5, 2))),
    "October 2025 WEO": ("#AD7CC5", (0, (2, 2))),
}
```

Each entry of the dictionary holds two things: a colour and a line style,
grouped in brackets as a *tuple*. Other scripts store just a colour per
series; when a series needs more than one setting, a tuple keeps them
together.

The latest vintage is solid and darkest, and older vintages are lighter and
broken. Using both colour and line style makes the chart readable in black
and white and for readers who find similar colours hard to tell apart.

A line style can be a name (`"solid"`, `"dashed"`, `"dotted"`) or a dash
pattern of the form `(offset, (on, off))`:

- **`(0, (5, 2))`**: dashes 5 line widths long with gaps of 2;
- **`(0, (2, 2))`**: shorter dashes with equal gaps, which look dotted at
  this line width.

The offset, 0, says where in the pattern the line starts. Dash lengths are
measured in line widths, so the pattern scales with the line. See [Line
styles](../techniques.qmd#sec-line-styles).

### The frame

The title is split over two lines before "Balance", and the caption has
seven lines describing the country definitions. `left=0.4` leaves room for
labels such as `-2.5`.

### The axis line and the lines

```python
# The x-axis is drawn at zero, with short tick marks pointing up; the year
# labels stay at the bottom of the chart.
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
ax.vlines(range(2021, 2032), 0, 0.04, color="black", linewidth=0.6)

for vintage, (colour, style) in vintages.items():
    ax.plot(years, data[vintage], color=colour, linestyle=style, linewidth=1.8,
            label=vintage)
```

Most values are negative, and the y-axis runs from -3 to 0.5. As in Excel's
*Horizontal axis crosses at 0*, the axis line is drawn at zero, near the top
of the plot, with a short tick for every year. The ticks are 0.04 high, in
data units. See [An axis line at zero](../techniques.qmd#sec-axis-line).

The loop unpacks each dictionary entry in one step:
`for vintage, (colour, style) in vintages.items()` gives the name, and splits
the tuple into `colour` and `style`. The brackets around `(colour, style)`
tell Python that the value is itself a pair. The line style is then passed
to `ax.plot()` with `linestyle=style`.

The newest vintage comes first in the dictionary, so it is drawn first and
the older ones lie on top of it where they overlap. For dashed lines that
works well: the solid line shows through the gaps.

### The axes

```python
ax.set_xlim(2021, 2031)
ax.set_xticks(range(2021, 2032, 2))
ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=0, pad=5)

set_y_scale(ax, -3, 0.5, 0.5)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter("{x:.1f}")
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)
```

- **Ticks and labels.** The tick marks at zero are at every year (from the
  `vlines` call above) but the labels only at every second year: 2021,
  2023, ..., 2031, as in the published chart.
- **No margin.** The x-limits are exactly the first and last year, so the
  lines run from edge to edge.
- **The bottom spine** and its tick marks are hidden, because the axis line
  is now at zero.
- **The y-axis** runs from -3 to 0.5 in steps of 0.5, so zero is a tick.
- **One decimal.** `ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter("{x:.1f}")` is a shortcut:
  give matplotlib a format string and it applies it to every label. `{x}`
  stands for the tick value and `:.1f` means one decimal, so the labels read
  -3.0, -2.5, ..., 0.5. This does the same as
  `FormatStrFormatter("%.1f")` in [Figure 2.1](fig-2-1.qmd), in the newer
  Python format style. See [Number
  formats](../techniques.qmd#sec-number-formats).

### The legend

```python
ax.legend(loc="lower right", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.03), handlelength=3.4,
          labelspacing=0.1)
```

The legend sits in the lower right, which the lines leave empty. It has
long sample lines (`handlelength=3.4`, against the default 2), so each dash
pattern repeats a few times and is recognisable. See
[Legends](../techniques.qmd#sec-legends).

## Changing the chart

- **A new vintage.** For the next edition, add `"April 2027 WEO"` at the top
  of the dictionary with the darkest colour and `"solid"`, and move the
  others down a step: the previous newest becomes dashed, and so on. If you
  keep only three, delete the oldest.
- **A dotted line with round dots.** Use `linestyle=(0, (0.1, 2))` together
  with `dash_capstyle="round"`. The very short dashes are drawn as dots.
- **Shading the projection years** would also help the reader: see the
  suggestion in [Figure 9.2](fig-9-2.qmd).

## The complete script

The full `python/fig-10-2.py`, as it runs:

```` {.python filename="python/fig-10-2.py"}
"""Figure 10.2: LA7: General Government Structural Primary Balance."""
from chart_style import new_chart, read_chart_data, save_chart, set_y_scale

STEM = "fig-10-2"

data = read_chart_data(STEM)
years = data["category"]

# Each vintage of the projections: (colour, line style).
vintages = {
    "October 2026 WEO": ("#5B267A", "solid"),
    "April 2026 WEO": ("#8752AA", (0, (5, 2))),
    "October 2025 WEO": ("#AD7CC5", (0, (2, 2))),
}

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="LA7: General Government Structural Primary\nBalance",
    subtitle="(Percent of potential GDP)",
    caption=(
        "Sources: IMF, World Economic Outlook database; and IMF staff\n"
        "calculations.\n"
        "Note: LA7 is simple average. Chile refers to the central government’s\n"
        "structural non-mining primary balance. Colombia refers to the\n"
        "consolidated public sector's structural non-oil primary balance. Peru refers\n"
        "to the nonfinancial public sector’s structural primary balance. LA7 = Latin\n"
        "America 7 (Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay)."
    ),
    left=0.4,
    right=0.2,
    bottom_gap=0.35,
)

# The x-axis is drawn at zero, with short tick marks pointing up; the year
# labels stay at the bottom of the chart.
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
ax.vlines(range(2021, 2032), 0, 0.04, color="black", linewidth=0.6)

for vintage, (colour, style) in vintages.items():
    ax.plot(years, data[vintage], color=colour, linestyle=style, linewidth=1.8,
            label=vintage)

ax.set_xlim(2021, 2031)
ax.set_xticks(range(2021, 2032, 2))
ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=0, pad=5)

set_y_scale(ax, -3, 0.5, 0.5)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter("{x:.1f}")
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)

ax.legend(loc="lower right", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.03), handlelength=3.4,
          labelspacing=0.1)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
````
